pages.title: Chapter Analysis
pages.triage_reason: Exam weightage and chapter overview; no mechanism to animate.

pages.title: Measuring Rate of Reaction
pages.triage_reason: Lists volume of gas, change in mass, and change in pressure as measurement methods; the graph reasoning is developed on pages 4 and 5.

pages.title: Calculating Rate of Reaction: Volume of Gas
pages.triage_reason: Links gas volume produced over time to graph gradient, falling rate, and completion.

pages.title: Calculating Rate of Reaction: Change in Mass
pages.triage_reason: Shows the same rate story through mass loss as escaping hydrogen makes the setup lighter.

pages.title: Conditions for Successful Reaction
pages.triage_reason: Section divider listing the five factors; the collision conditions and factors are represented on later pages.

pages.title: Conditions for Effective Collision
pages.triage_reason: Defines effective collision as needing both sufficient energy and the right orientation.

pages.title: Five Factors That Affect Rate of Reaction
pages.triage_reason: Lists the five factors; each factor is given a more source-grounded artifact on pages 9 to 13.

pages.title: Size of Reactant Particles
pages.triage_reason: Explains smaller particles through greater exposed surface area and higher frequency of effective collisions.

pages.title: Concentration of Reactants
pages.triage_reason: Connects higher concentration to more particles per unit volume, steeper initial gradient, and unchanged final gas volume when the limiting reagent is unchanged.

pages.title: Pressure Applied
pages.triage_reason: Explains higher pressure as decreased volume, closer gas particles, and more frequent effective collisions.

pages.title: Temperature of System
pages.triage_reason: Shows that higher temperature increases particle speed and the fraction of particles with energy at least activation energy.

pages.title: Use of Catalysts
pages.triage_reason: Explains an alternative pathway with lower activation energy and the resulting higher chance of effective collision.

pages.title: Biological Catalyst: Enzymes
pages.triage_reason: Defines enzymes and lists characteristics; the PDF does not develop enzyme binding or denaturation enough for a separate mechanism artifact.

pages.title: TYS Question: Activation Energy
pages.triage_reason: TYS question asks how activation energy changes with catalyst versus increased temperature; this is built into the catalyst artifact.

pages.title: TYS Question: Concentration Graph
pages.triage_reason: TYS question asks students to choose the curve for higher acid concentration with the same magnesium mass and acid in excess.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: As reactants are used up, effective collisions become less frequent, so gas volume rises more slowly or mass falls more slowly until the graph gradient is zero.
artifacts.transferable_principle: For rate of reaction graphs, the gradient at a time tells the rate at that time; the initial gradient gives the initial rate.

steps.name: Start fast
steps.beat: At the start there are many reactant particles, so the graph has its steepest gradient.

steps.name: Collect evidence
steps.beat: Gas collection rises with time, while mass of the setup falls if gas escapes.

steps.name: Rate falls
steps.beat: As reactants are used up, the graph becomes gentler because less gas is produced per unit time.

steps.name: Reaction complete
steps.beat: When no more gas is produced, the graph becomes horizontal and the gradient is zero.

key_symbols.meaning: The macroscopic measurement of gas volume produced.
The macroscopic measurement of mass lost as gas escapes.
The steep early gradient used to read initial rate.
The zero-gradient region showing that the reaction is complete.
The microscopic reason the rate decreases over time.

interactivity_hooks: Scrub reaction time to connect particle depletion to the changing graph gradient.
Switch between gas volume and mass loss to compare the same rate pattern.
Toggle a tangent marker to estimate initial rate from the first part of the graph.

artifact_metadata.title: Gradient Tells the Rate
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Rate of reaction: measuring volume of gas produced and change in mass over time

learning_design.core_aha: I can read a reaction's speed from how steep the graph is, not just from how high or low the graph looks.
learning_objectives: Identify initial rate as the initial gradient of a product-time graph.
Explain why the gradient becomes gentler as reactants are used up.
Recognise zero gradient as the reaction being complete.
Relate gas volume and mass loss graphs to the same rate of reaction.

target_misconceptions.misconception: The reaction is fastest when the graph has the largest gas volume.
target_misconceptions.correction: The reaction is fastest where the graph is steepest, usually at the start.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A horizontal graph means the gas has disappeared.
target_misconceptions.correction: A horizontal graph means no more gas is being produced; the final amount remains present or measured.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A mass-loss graph and gas-volume graph show unrelated trends.
target_misconceptions.correction: They measure the same reaction from opposite macroscopic signals: gas gained in the syringe or mass lost from the flask.

representations.description: Students link animated particles, a lab measurement, and a live graph with tangent gradient readouts.

views.description: Animated reactant particles collide less often as the reaction proceeds and particles are used up.
A gas syringe fills or a balance reading decreases while time passes.
A volume-time or mass-time graph draws live with tangent gradient, initial rate, and zero-gradient plateau labels.

scenarios.title: Find the Initial Rate
scenarios.guiding_question: Where is the gas-volume graph steepest, and what does that say about the initial rate?
scenarios.success_criterion: You identify the first tangent as the steepest part and call it the initial rate.

scenarios.title: Spot Completion
scenarios.guiding_question: How do you know from the graph that no further reaction is occurring?
scenarios.success_criterion: You pause at the plateau and explain that zero gradient means no more gas is produced.

scenarios.title: Change the Measurement
scenarios.guiding_question: What stays similar when the same reaction is measured by gas volume instead of mass loss?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that both graphs are steepest at the start and become zero-gradient at completion.

scenarios.title: Build a Rate Story
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you make a faster or slower reaction and still explain it using gradient?
scenarios.success_criterion: You describe the particle collisions, the macroscopic reading, and the graph gradient in one linked sentence.

checkpoints.prompt: Complete the summary: rate of reaction is shown by the graph ______; the initial rate is the ______ gradient.
Match each measurement to the graph signal it produces.

ui_requirements.tone: Exam-focused, visual, and precise without adding vocabulary beyond the notes.
accessibility: Do not rely on colour alone for steep and gentle gradients.
Provide pause and scrub controls for animation.
Label graph axes directly.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Reacting particles form products only when a collision has sufficient energy and the correct orientation; missing either condition makes the collision ineffective.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Every rate factor should be explained by how it changes the frequency of effective collisions.

steps.name: Particles approach
steps.beat: Reactant particles move and collide in an animated microscopic view.

steps.name: Check energy
steps.beat: A collision must have energy greater than or equal to the activation energy.

steps.name: Check orientation
steps.beat: The particles must meet in the right orientation for bonds to change.

steps.name: Form products
steps.beat: Only collisions that pass both checks count as effective collisions and produce products.

key_symbols.meaning: Shows whether the collision has sufficient energy.
Shows whether the particles meet in the right orientation.
The minimum energy needed for reaction.
Counts successful collisions that form products.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle collision energy and orientation to test whether products form.
Watch non-effective collisions bounce apart with a reason label.
Compare total collisions with successful collisions.

artifact_metadata.title: Two Gates for an Effective Collision
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Collision theory: sufficient energy and right orientation for effective collision

learning_design.core_aha: A collision is not automatically successful; I need both enough energy and the right orientation before products form.
learning_objectives: State the two conditions for an effective collision.
Distinguish total collision frequency from effective collision frequency.
Explain why insufficient energy or wrong orientation prevents product formation.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Any collision between reactants forms products.
target_misconceptions.correction: Only effective collisions form products; ineffective collisions do not lead to reaction.
The particles also need the right orientation for the collision to be effective.
The collision must also have enough energy to overcome activation energy.

representations.description: A two-gate model links particle collisions, product formation, and symbolic condition checks.

views.description: Particles move, collide, bounce apart, or react depending on energy and orientation.
A visible product counter rises only when a collision is successful.
A symbolic checklist and activation energy marker show which condition passes or fails.

scenarios.title: Right Orientation, Low Energy
scenarios.guiding_question: If the particles face the right way but do not reach activation energy, should products form?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that correct orientation is not enough when energy is below activation energy.

scenarios.title: Enough Energy, Wrong Orientation
scenarios.guiding_question: Why does a high-energy collision still fail when the particles meet in the wrong orientation?
scenarios.success_criterion: You state that sufficient energy must be paired with the right orientation.

scenarios.title: Make It Effective
scenarios.guiding_question: Which two settings must both be true before the collision becomes a successful collision?
scenarios.success_criterion: You set energy at or above activation energy and choose right orientation, then products form.

scenarios.title: Collision Counter Challenge
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you create many collisions but only a few effective collisions, then explain why?
scenarios.success_criterion: You distinguish collision frequency from effective collision frequency using the counters.

checkpoints.prompt: An effective collision needs sufficient ______ and the right ______.
A collision has enough energy but the wrong orientation. What happens?
options: Products form because energy is enough
No products form because the collision is not effective
checkpoints.answer: No products form because the collision is not effective

ui_requirements.tone: Use clear O-Level collision-theory language and avoid molecular detail beyond the notes.
accessibility: Use icons and labels for pass or fail states.
Let students pause individual collision replays.
Pair animation changes with text reason chips.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Smaller reactant particles expose a greater total surface area, so more reactant particles can collide effectively per unit time and the reaction is faster.
artifacts.transferable_principle: For the same amount of solid, increasing exposed surface area increases the frequency of effective collisions.

steps.name: Same amount
steps.beat: Begin with the same mass or amount of solid reactant.

steps.name: Break into pieces
steps.beat: Smaller pieces expose more total surface area to the other reactant.

steps.name: More exposed collisions
steps.beat: More particles can collide at the solid surface in the same time.

steps.name: Faster reaction
steps.beat: The higher frequency of effective collisions gives a steeper initial gradient.

key_symbols.meaning: A solid with less exposed surface area.
The same solid split into smaller particles with more exposed surface.
The parts of the solid available for collisions.
Effective collisions occurring at the exposed surface.
Reminds students not to confuse faster rate with more product when amount is unchanged.

interactivity_hooks: Change particle size while keeping the amount of solid fixed.
Animate particles striking only exposed solid surfaces.
Compare initial gradient and final product amount for lump, chips, and powder.

artifact_metadata.title: Smaller Pieces, More Surface
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Factors affecting rate: size of reactant particles and total surface area

learning_design.core_aha: Smaller solid particles react faster because more surface is exposed for effective collisions, not because the solid suddenly has more mass.
learning_objectives: Compare large and small particle sizes by total exposed surface area.
Explain why smaller particles increase the frequency of effective collisions.
Predict the graph with a steeper initial gradient when particle size decreases.
Separate faster rate from greater final amount when the amount of solid is unchanged.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Powder reacts faster because there is more reactant.
target_misconceptions.correction: For the same amount, powder reacts faster because more surface area is exposed.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Only the outside shape changes; collision frequency should stay the same.
target_misconceptions.correction: More exposed surface gives more places for reacting particles to collide effectively.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A faster reaction must produce a larger final volume of gas.
target_misconceptions.correction: If the amount of limiting reactant is unchanged, the final product amount stays the same.

representations.description: The artifact connects exposed solid surface, visible reaction speed, and graph gradient.

views.description: Animated particles strike exposed surfaces of a lump, chips, or powder and count effective collisions.
A reaction vessel shows bubbles forming faster for smaller particles under the same amount of solid.
A live product-time graph compares initial gradient and final plateau for each particle size.

scenarios.title: Keep the Amount Fixed
scenarios.guiding_question: If the same amount of solid is used, what actually changes when a lump becomes powder?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that surface area changes while the amount of solid stays fixed.

scenarios.title: Reveal Collision Sites
scenarios.guiding_question: Where can collisions happen, and why does powder give more effective collisions per second?
scenarios.success_criterion: You link the highlighted exposed surface to a higher effective collision frequency.

scenarios.title: Choose the Faster Curve
scenarios.guiding_question: Which particle size gives the steepest initial gradient, and should the final plateau change?
scenarios.success_criterion: You choose powder for the steepest initial gradient and keep the final plateau tied to amount.

scenarios.title: Surface Area Lab
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you make the reaction faster and separately make more final product?
scenarios.success_criterion: You use particle size to change rate and amount of solid to change final product amount.

checkpoints.prompt: Smaller particles have greater total ______ area, causing a higher frequency of ______ collisions.
The same mass of powder reacts faster than one large lump because powder has:
options: a greater total exposed surface area
checkpoints.answer: a greater total exposed surface area

ui_requirements.tone: Concrete and lab-like, with repeated reminders that amount and surface area are different variables.
accessibility: Use outlines and labels for exposed surface areas.
Provide text counters alongside animated collision sparks.
Keep graph curves visibly distinct without relying only on colour.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.topic: Concentration, initial gradient, and final volume
artifacts.mechanism: Higher concentration puts more reacting particles in the same volume, increasing collision frequency and initial rate while final gas volume stays the same if the limiting reagent amount is unchanged.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Changing concentration changes rate through particles per unit volume; changing the limiting reagent amount changes the final amount of product.

steps.name: Pack more particles
steps.beat: A higher concentration means more reacting particles in the same volume.

steps.name: Collide more often
steps.beat: More particles per unit volume gives a higher collision frequency.

steps.name: Start steeper
steps.beat: The graph has a steeper initial gradient because the initial rate is higher.

steps.name: Check the plateau
steps.beat: If the limiting reagent amount is the same, the final gas volume stays the same.

steps.name: Choose the curve
steps.beat: For the TYS graph, pick the curve with a steeper initial gradient but the same plateau.

key_symbols.meaning: The lower concentration comparison from the graph question.
The higher concentration with more particles per unit volume.
The TYS curve with faster initial rate and same final volume.
Shows unchanged final gas volume when magnesium amount is unchanged and acid is in excess.
Distractors that change final volume instead of only rate.

interactivity_hooks: Change acid concentration and watch particle density, collision frequency, and initial gradient respond together.
Lock magnesium at 0.5 g to show why final hydrogen volume stays the same when acid is in excess.
Try TYS curve choices A to D and receive feedback on gradient and plateau.

artifact_metadata.title: More Concentrated, Steeper Start
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Factors affecting rate: concentration of reactants and interpretation of gas-volume graphs

learning_design.core_aha: A higher concentration makes the graph start steeper, but it does not change the final gas volume when the limiting reagent is unchanged.
learning_objectives: Explain higher concentration as more particles per unit volume.
Link higher collision frequency to a steeper initial gradient.
Use limiting reagent reasoning to predict the same final gas volume.
Choose the correct TYS graph for 2.0 mol/dm3 acid under the same conditions.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A higher concentration always produces more gas.
target_misconceptions.correction: It produces gas faster, but the final volume stays the same if the same limiting reagent amount is used.

target_misconceptions.misconception: The correct graph is the one with the highest plateau.
target_misconceptions.correction: For the TYS question, the correct graph has the same plateau and a steeper initial gradient.
Concentration changes collision frequency, not the activation energy barrier.

representations.description: Students compare concentration through particle density, live gas production, and TYS-style curve selection.

views.description: Animated particles crowd into the same volume as concentration increases, causing more collisions per second.
A 0.5 g magnesium ribbon reacts with excess hydrochloric acid while hydrogen volume is collected.
A gas-volume graph overlays curves A to D with initial gradient and final plateau checks.

scenarios.title: More Particles in Same Volume
scenarios.guiding_question: What changes inside the same volume when concentration increases from 1.0 to 2.0 mol/dm3?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain higher concentration as more particles per unit volume and higher collision frequency.

scenarios.title: Keep Magnesium Fixed
scenarios.guiding_question: Why does the final hydrogen volume stay the same when 0.5 g magnesium reacts with excess acid?
scenarios.success_criterion: You state that magnesium is the limiting reagent, so changing excess acid concentration changes rate but not final volume.

scenarios.title: Pick the TYS Curve
scenarios.guiding_question: Which curve shows 2.0 mol/dm3 acid with the same 0.5 g magnesium under the same conditions?
scenarios.success_criterion: You choose B because it has a steeper initial gradient but the same final gas volume as graph 1.

scenarios.title: Rate or Amount
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you change rate without changing final amount, then change final amount deliberately?
scenarios.success_criterion: You use concentration for initial rate and magnesium mass for final hydrogen volume.

checkpoints.prompt: Higher concentration increases collision ______ and gives a steeper initial ______, while the final volume stays the same if the limiting reagent is unchanged.
In the TYS graph question, why is B correct?
options: It has a higher final plateau
It has a lower final plateau
It is steeper at the start but reaches the same final volume
It is less steep but eventually catches up
checkpoints.answer: It is steeper at the start but reaches the same final volume

ui_requirements.tone: Exam-strategy focused: every graph choice must pass both gradient and plateau checks.
accessibility: Use dashed and solid curve styles plus labels A to D.
Provide text feedback for each wrong curve choice.
Keep units visible as mol/dm3 and g.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: For gaseous reactants, higher pressure decreases volume and brings particles closer together, giving more particles per unit volume and a higher frequency of effective collisions.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Increasing gas pressure speeds a reaction by increasing particle density, not by changing the chemical identity of the reactants.

steps.name: Compress the gas
steps.beat: Higher pressure is shown by the same gas particles occupying a smaller volume.

steps.name: Particles get closer
steps.beat: The number of particles per unit volume increases.

steps.name: Collisions increase
steps.beat: Closer particles collide more frequently.

steps.name: Rate rises
steps.beat: More frequent effective collisions increase the rate of reaction.

key_symbols.meaning: Compresses the gas to raise pressure.
Shows pressure changes volume rather than adding particles.
Visible successful collisions per unit time.
Displays more reactants per unit volume at higher pressure.

interactivity_hooks: Move a piston to change pressure and particle spacing.
Lock particle number to make particle density visible.
Compare collision frequency counters at low and high pressure.

artifact_metadata.title: Pressure Packs Gas Particles Closer
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Factors affecting rate: pressure applied to gaseous reactants

learning_design.core_aha: Higher pressure speeds gas reactions because the same particles are packed closer together, so they collide effectively more often.
learning_objectives: Describe higher pressure as lower volume for gaseous reactants.
Explain more particles per unit volume at higher pressure.
Link particle density to higher collision frequency and rate of reaction.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Increasing pressure adds more reactant particles.
target_misconceptions.correction: The page explains pressure as bringing existing particles closer together by decreasing volume.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Pressure affects solids and liquids in the same way as gases for this topic.
target_misconceptions.correction: This pressure explanation is for gaseous reactants whose volume can be compressed.

representations.description: A piston animation connects gas compression to collision frequency and a steeper symbolic rate graph.

views.description: Animated gas particles move in a box whose volume changes with pressure.
A piston or syringe compresses gaseous reactants while a pressure readout increases.
A particle-density meter and rate graph show higher pressure causing a steeper initial gradient.

scenarios.title: Compress Without Adding
scenarios.guiding_question: When pressure increases, what happens to volume and particle spacing if the particle count stays the same?
scenarios.success_criterion: You state that volume decreases and particles become closer together without adding particles.

scenarios.title: Count the Collisions
scenarios.guiding_question: How does the collision frequency change when gas particles are closer together?
scenarios.success_criterion: You connect smaller volume to more collisions per second and a faster rate of reaction.

scenarios.title: Name the State
scenarios.guiding_question: Why does this pressure explanation belong to gaseous reactants?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that gases can be compressed so particles per unit volume changes clearly.

scenarios.title: Pressure Simulator
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you raise collision frequency using pressure and explain each visual change?
scenarios.success_criterion: You link pressure, volume, particles per unit volume, collision frequency, and rate of reaction.

checkpoints.prompt: Higher pressure brings gas particles ______ together because the volume is ______.
Match each pressure idea to the rate explanation.

ui_requirements.tone: Mechanistic and restrained, emphasising gaseous reactants and particle spacing.
accessibility: Use numeric readouts for pressure, volume, and collision frequency.
Make split-view comparisons available without animation.
Label gas state explicitly.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: Increasing temperature raises average kinetic energy, so particles move faster and a larger fraction have energy greater than or equal to activation energy, increasing effective collision frequency.
artifacts.transferable_principle: Temperature affects rate in two linked ways: faster particle motion and a larger enough-energy fraction.

steps.name: Heat the system
steps.beat: The average kinetic energy of particles increases.

steps.name: Move faster
steps.beat: Particles travel faster and collide more often.

steps.name: Clear the barrier
steps.beat: A larger fraction of particles has energy at least equal to activation energy.

steps.name: Rate increases
steps.beat: More frequent effective collisions make the reaction faster.

key_symbols.meaning: Raises average kinetic energy in the system.
Shows particles moving faster at higher temperature.
The energy threshold particles must meet or exceed.
The larger fraction of particles able to react at higher temperature.

interactivity_hooks: Raise temperature to speed up particles in the collision box.
Watch the shaded fraction above activation energy grow on the energy view.
Compare collision frequency with effective collision frequency.

artifact_metadata.title: Temperature Gives Two Rate Boosts
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Factors affecting rate: temperature of system and activation energy

learning_design.core_aha: Heating does not lower activation energy; it gives more particles enough kinetic energy to overcome the same barrier.
learning_objectives: Describe how higher temperature increases average kinetic energy.
Explain why faster particles collide more frequently.
Use an activation energy line to compare the fraction of particles able to react.
Avoid confusing temperature increase with catalyst action.

target_misconceptions.correction: The activation energy stays the same; more particles have enough energy to overcome it.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Temperature only makes particles collide more often.
target_misconceptions.correction: Higher temperature also increases the fraction of particles with energy at least activation energy.

representations.description: Students see the two temperature effects in particle motion and in an energy distribution with an activation energy line.

views.description: Particles move faster at higher temperature, producing more collisions and more effective collisions.
A reaction vessel with a thermometer shows the system being heated and product forming faster.
A live energy distribution keeps the activation energy line fixed while the enough-energy fraction changes.

scenarios.title: Heat and Watch Motion
scenarios.guiding_question: What happens to particle speed and collision frequency when temperature increases?
scenarios.success_criterion: You state that higher temperature gives particles more kinetic energy, so they move faster and collide more often.

scenarios.title: Count Particles Above Ea
scenarios.guiding_question: How does heating change the fraction of particles with energy greater than or equal to activation energy?
scenarios.success_criterion: You identify the shaded enough-energy fraction as larger at higher temperature.

scenarios.title: Does Ea Move?
scenarios.guiding_question: When temperature increases, does the activation energy barrier itself become lower?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that activation energy stays fixed while more particles have enough energy.

scenarios.title: Temperature Lab
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you predict the fastest setting using both particle speed and enough-energy fraction?
scenarios.success_criterion: You justify the rate using both collision frequency and the fraction above activation energy.

checkpoints.prompt: Match each temperature effect to its rate consequence.
What happens to activation energy when temperature is increased?

ui_requirements.tone: Precise and misconception-aware, especially about temperature versus catalyst effects.
accessibility: Use numeric percentage labels for the enough-energy fraction.
Allow reduced-motion mode with stepped particle positions.
Keep the activation energy line labelled at all times.

artifacts.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifacts.mechanism: A catalyst provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy, so more reacting particles have sufficient kinetic energy and effective collisions become more likely.
artifacts.transferable_principle: A catalyst changes the route and rate of reaction without changing final yield or being chemically altered.

steps.name: Original pathway
steps.beat: Without a catalyst, particles must overcome a higher activation energy barrier.

steps.name: Alternative pathway
steps.beat: The catalyst provides a route with lower activation energy.

steps.name: More particles qualify
steps.beat: More particles now have sufficient kinetic energy to overcome the lower barrier.

steps.name: Rate increases
steps.beat: Effective collisions become more likely, but the catalyst is not chemically altered and yield is unchanged.

steps.name: TYS distinction
steps.beat: A catalyst decreases activation energy; increasing temperature does not.

key_symbols.meaning: The original higher activation energy route.
The alternative lower activation energy route.
The key change caused by the catalyst.
Prevents students from thinking the catalyst increases final product amount.
Catalyst decreases activation energy while increased temperature leaves activation energy unchanged.

interactivity_hooks: Toggle a catalyst to lower the activation energy on an energy profile diagram.
Compare the fraction of particles above the uncatalysed and catalysed barriers.
Answer the TYS catalyst-versus-temperature activation energy question with feedback.

artifact_metadata.title: Catalyst Lowers the Barrier
artifact_metadata.subject: O Level Chemistry
artifact_metadata.syllabus_reference: Factors affecting rate: catalysts, alternative pathway, and activation energy

learning_design.core_aha: A catalyst speeds the reaction by lowering activation energy through an alternative pathway, while temperature speeds it without lowering that barrier.
learning_objectives: Describe a catalyst as providing an alternative reaction pathway with lower activation energy.
Explain why a lower activation energy increases the chance of effective collision.
State that a catalyst is not chemically altered and does not change yield.
Answer the TYS activation-energy comparison for catalyst and temperature.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst gives particles more kinetic energy.
target_misconceptions.correction: A catalyst lowers the activation energy barrier; it does not heat the particles.

target_misconceptions.misconception: Increasing temperature lowers activation energy in the same way as a catalyst.
target_misconceptions.correction: Temperature increases particle kinetic energy, but activation energy stays the same.

target_misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst increases the yield or is used up by the reaction.
target_misconceptions.correction: The notes state that yield is not altered and the catalyst is not chemically altered.

representations.description: Students link catalyst pathway, enough-energy fraction, and TYS table reasoning.

views.description: Animated collisions show more particles becoming effective when the energy barrier is lowered.
A small amount of catalyst is added; product forms faster while final yield and catalyst amount indicators stay unchanged.
An energy profile diagram compares uncatalysed and catalysed pathways with activation energy arrows.
A TYS table contrasts catalyst addition with temperature increase and highlights answer B.

scenarios.title: Add the Catalyst
scenarios.guiding_question: What changes on the energy profile when a catalyst is added?
scenarios.success_criterion: You explain that the catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower activation energy.

scenarios.title: More Particles Over the Barrier
scenarios.guiding_question: Why does lowering activation energy make effective collisions more likely?
scenarios.success_criterion: You connect the lower barrier to a higher number of particles with sufficient kinetic energy.

scenarios.title: Catalyst or Temperature?
scenarios.guiding_question: In the TYS table, what happens to activation energy for a catalyst and for an increase in temperature?
scenarios.success_criterion: You choose B: catalyst decreases activation energy, while increased temperature leaves activation energy the same.

scenarios.title: Check Yield and Catalyst
scenarios.guiding_question: What should stay unchanged even though the reaction is faster with a catalyst?
scenarios.success_criterion: You state that yield is not altered and the catalyst is not chemically altered.

scenarios.title: Barrier Compare
scenarios.guiding_question: Can you make the reaction faster using a catalyst, then explain how that differs from heating?
scenarios.success_criterion: You compare catalyst and temperature using activation energy, kinetic energy, and effective collision frequency.

checkpoints.prompt: A catalyst provides an alternative pathway with lower ______ energy.
Which TYS row is correct for activation energy?
options: B: catalyst decreases, temperature stays the same
D: catalyst increases, temperature stays the same
checkpoints.answer: B: catalyst decreases, temperature stays the same

checkpoints.prompt: Match each catalyst statement to the notes-based meaning.

ui_requirements.tone: Exam-ready and careful about catalyst versus temperature distinctions.
accessibility: Use labelled arrows for both activation energy barriers.
Show TYS feedback in text as well as highlights.
Keep catalyst and temperature controls visually separate.

house_style.layout: header, two-column stage/sidebar, caption bar, controls, steps list, reference panels
